articles.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
articles.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.
articles.content:
Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil. Researchers at Virginia Tech have developed a new chemical process that transforms one of the world's most difficult plastics to recycle into a high-performance lubricant material.

Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.

Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.

PVC is particularly difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content and the wide range of chemical additives manufacturers incorporate into their products. These additives can give PVC different properties, such as flexibility, rigidity, and resistance to heat. However, they also complicate conventional recycling methods. Consequently, much of the world's discarded PVC ends up in landfills.

Turning Plastic Waste Into High-Performance Lubricants

Meanwhile, global demand for lubricants continues to grow, and producing these materials can come with significant environmental costs. Transforming discarded PVC into a valuable lubricant ingredient could help address both problems.

Although lubricants rarely attract much attention, they are essential to modern machinery. They reduce friction and wear between moving components, helping engines operate efficiently and extending the lifespan of mechanical equipment. Everything from lawn mowers and passenger vehicles to jet engines depends on reliable lubricants.

The Virginia Tech team's process could provide an alternative source of these important materials while helping address the growing problem of plastic pollution.

To make the lubricant, researchers place PVC of the kind commonly used in household plumbing, window frames, and credit cards into a solvent. They then introduce aluminum trichloride and alpha-olefins, a class of hydrocarbons used in the manufacture of synthetic lubricants. The mixture is heated to 158 degrees Fahrenheit for three hours, after which the researchers extract a relatively thick lubricating oil.

The resulting polyalphaolefin belongs to a family of synthetic base oils valued for their stability, lubricating properties, and ability to perform across a wide range of temperatures. These materials are commonly used as the foundation for high-performance synthetic engine oils.

"Number one, we have proved that it is feasible to use plastic waste to make high-performance lubricants. Number two, these lubricants are green, and they can meet the emerging needs for sustainability by the market," Liu said.

Building on Earlier Plastic Recycling Breakthroughs

The discovery grew out of previous research by Liu's laboratory, published in Science and Nature Sustainability. In those studies, the researchers demonstrated how other types of plastic waste could be transformed into surfactants, substances that help water interact with oils and grease and are widely used in soaps and detergents.

Encouraged by those successes, the researchers decided to tackle the more challenging problem of PVC waste.

"We want to help improve the recycling and upcycling of PVC," Liu said.

Unlike conventional recycling, which typically aims to recover materials for reuse, upcycling seeks to transform discarded materials into products with greater value or usefulness.

Liu recruited a group of graduate researchers to investigate this possibility. Eric Munyaneza Nuwayo, who was completing the final year of his doctoral program, was selected to lead the project. Connor S. Thompson, a chemistry graduate student who had been pursuing a different research topic, joined the effort after Liu suggested changing direction.

Abby Civiello, a graduate student in her first year, also joined the team and quickly became an important contributor to the research.

"I often called them the three musketeers," Liu said.

An Unexpected Discovery in Polymer Chemistry

The researchers initially experimented with ways to modify the molecular structure of PVC and convert it into more useful substances.

Like other plastics, PVC is a polymer, meaning it consists of long molecular chains made up of repeating chemical units. The researchers initially hoped that changing the chemical groups attached to these chains would produce a material with desirable properties.

"The idea was simple. PVC, as one of the most activated forms of polyethylene, ought to be easily converted into some other molecules by replacing the chlorine atoms with other groups," Liu said.

However, the early experiments consistently produced disappointing results. Instead of creating a functional material with the desired performance characteristics, the team ended up with soft, sticky substances that had little practical value.

Those frustrating results eventually inspired Liu to approach the problem differently. Rather than continuing to modify the long molecular chains, he wondered whether breaking them into smaller pieces might produce something more useful.

"One day I realized -- if this polymer is so gooey and so soft, why don't I just keep breaking the polymer chains down to smaller segments?" said Liu.

As the researchers refined their chemical process and evaluated the properties of the materials it produced, Liu began to recognize that the team had discovered something with implications extending well beyond plastic recycling.

They had found a potential new route for manufacturing valuable industrial lubricants.

Bringing Recycled Plastic Lubricants to the Market

To better understand the properties and commercial potential of the new oil, Liu enlisted the expertise of researchers at several institutions.

He provided samples to Ali Erdemir at Texas A&M University, where researchers evaluated the performance of the finished materials. William Goddard at the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech, contributed chemical computations to help investigate the underlying chemistry.

At Virginia Tech, Xi Chen examined the economic and manufacturing aspects of the technology, developing models to explore how the oil could be produced on a larger scale.

The research establishes that discarded PVC can serve as a starting material for producing high-performance lubricants. However, expanding the process beyond the laboratory remains an important next step.

Liu hopes to further improve the environmental sustainability of the technology while making the resulting lubricants more widely available. Ultimately, the approach could give one of the world's most problematic plastics a valuable second life and provide industries with an alternative source of essential lubricating materials.

"Lubricants are the silent hero out there. We often don't recognize they exist, but they are out there working quietly. We want to be able to produce the oil on a larger scale to reach more people in the world," Liu said.

The impact is broad, benefiting environmental sustainability and industrial manufacturing, with detailed context and potential for large-scale application.

articles.title: Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy
articles.summary: The islands, being planted in five Glasgow parks, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.
articles.content:
Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.

The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.

The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.

Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.
articles.reasoning: The story reports a tangible environmental initiative with broad public benefit, creating new wildlife habitats and improving water quality in multiple public parks as part of a major event legacy, with clear details on scope and impact.

**Impact** – The project will add nearly 250 square metres of new habitats for wildlife. These islands also improve water quality by filtering it naturally. The installations are expected to last around 20 years, providing long-term benefits.

**What's next step** – The Glasgow 2026 organizers are funding this work as part of their promise to make the Games greener. The success of these islands could inspire similar projects in other cities or parks.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Glasgow’s floating nature islands create new homes for wildlife and help clean park waters as part of the city’s 2026 Games environmental plan.

articles.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
articles.summary: Officials say no lead has been detected in the surrounding area, which continues to be tested following concerns from locals.
articles.content:
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the controlled detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa: an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday following the detonation around the ammunition plant, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

An all-clear was issued. Local soil, air and water continue to be tested.

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.

In an update late on Wednesday, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead after the controlled explosion.

He wrote on X that the agency would "continue to be radically transparent with the public as sample results come in from the laboratory", and that these were "projected to start arriving back over the next 24 to 48 hours".

His post added: "Our goal is to complete ALL sampling by tomorrow and will remain on the ground to complete any remediation if at all necessary."

More than 1,000 post-detonation samples had been taken from homes, parks, farms and drinking water taps among other locations, Zeldin said. On Thursday, sites including churches, schools and playgrounds would be sampled as well.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a successful controlled detonation of toxic explosives with no detected lead contamination, ongoing environmental monitoring, and transparency efforts. This represents a meaningful environmental safety achievement with broad public health implications for the local community and potentially sets a precedent for handling similar hazardous materials safely.
articles.personality_title: US Army successfully detonates toxic explosives in Iowa with no lead contamination detected
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The US Army planned a controlled explosion of nearly five tonnes of a dangerous chemical called lead azide near an ammunition plant in Iowa. This chemical can explode on its own and posed safety concerns for the local community.

**What happened** – On Wednesday morning, the Army carried out the controlled blast after several delays caused by public worries and legal questions. Smoke was seen rising shortly after 9:00 a.m. local time. Officials quickly declared the risk of harm to be almost zero and gave an all-clear.

**Impact** – Tests done after the blast found no lead in the air, soil, or water nearby. Over 1,000 samples were taken from homes, parks, farms, and drinking water sources. This careful monitoring shows the explosion was handled safely and did not harm the environment or public health.

**What's next step** – The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will keep testing more places like schools, churches, and playgrounds. They plan to finish all tests by the next day and will clean up if any problems are found. The EPA promises to share all test results openly with the public.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The US Army’s careful explosion of toxic explosives in Iowa was successful and showed no lead pollution, with ongoing tests ensuring community safety.

articles.title: Expect fewer frosts and more hot days as UK seasons shift, says Met Office
articles.summary: Changing seasons are affecting wildlife and leading some farmers to grow different crops.
articles.content:
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.

Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.

In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.

The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.

"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.

"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.

"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."

The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant climate change impacts in the UK, highlighting measurable shifts in seasonal weather patterns that affect wildlife and agriculture. This has broad societal and environmental significance, providing important context on climate trends and their real-world effects.
articles.personality_title: UK winters have fewer frosts and summers get hotter, says Met Office
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The UK is experiencing changes in its seasons because of climate change. Winters are becoming milder with fewer frosty days, and summers are getting hotter with more warm days.

**What happened** – The Met Office, the UK's weather and climate agency, studied weather data from recent years and compared it to older records from 1961 to 1990. They found that the number of winter days with frost has dropped by about 25% across the UK, and in southern England, it has dropped by about 33%. At the same time, the number of summer days when temperatures reach 25°C or higher has more than doubled.

**Impact** – These changes are not just about the weather. They affect animals and plants because they rely on certain seasonal patterns to live and grow. For example, some wild animals may have to adjust their habits, and farmers are starting to plant different crops that suit the new weather better.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to watch how these seasonal changes develop. Farmers and wildlife experts will also adapt to find new ways to live with the changing climate. This ongoing monitoring helps people prepare for future weather patterns.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UK’s seasons are shifting with fewer frosty winters and hotter summers, affecting nature and farming in clear, measurable ways.
